implementation_notes: C# has no inline keyword; the JIT decides, and it inlines aggressively for small methods at hot call sites within and across methods in the same assembly. Cross-assembly inlining is possible in .NET (cross-assembly inlining was added and refined over several runtimes) but is more limited, so a genuinely hot small helper in a library is best expressed as a generic method (which is shared and specialised per call site, like a C++ template) rather than a normal method - the .NET team's own performance guidance recommends preferring generics over non-generic code for exactly this reason. AggressiveInlining is a method-level attribute that marks a method as hot for the JIT; it is mostly a legacy hint and modern .NET inlines based on profile data anyway. The bigger lever on .NET is usually avoiding the allocation (boxing, closures) rather than the call, and struct layout / [StructLayout] for locality.
idiom_name: JIT inlining of small methods; generic methods for cross-assembly specialisation; MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining
pitfalls: AggressiveInlining is largely a legacy hint; modern .NET JITs use profile data and inlining is mostly automatic for small methods.
Generic methods share code for reference types but specialise (and inline) for value types - the specialisation is per value type, so many value types mean many copies.
A megamorphic call site (many implementations at one site) defeats the JIT's inline cache and no amount of inlining the callee helps.
Boxing on the call boundary can cost more than the call itself - check the allocation profile before forcing inlining.
The debug build inlines far less than release, so an inlining measurement must be taken on the release build.
